title: You Don't Need More Willpower. You Need a Constitution.
author: Camilo Zambrano
summary: Camilo Zambrano proposes that the antidote to failed willpower-based self-discipline is not more grit but a written "personal constitution," borrowing the concept directly from organizational governance documents like Amazon's Leadership Principles and Anthropic's public AI constitution. He defines the document as three elements: a mission (the ultimate goal), a set of principles (fundamental decision-making guidelines), and a personal declaration (the reminder of why it matters), arguing this structure anchors identity and speeds judgment rather than enforcing rigid rules. Zambrano walks through a worked example, using his own hypothetical constitution to filter a stress-response decision (gym, writing, meditation, cooking, wine, casino, or partying) down to the option that best satisfies competing principles simultaneously. The piece closes by extending the concept from individuals to families, describing how he and his wife are building shared household principles, like refusing to scream during conflict, that function as an informal family constitution for their children.
points: Defines a personal constitution as three concrete elements (mission, principles, personal declaration), directly modeled on organizational documents like Amazon's Leadership Principles and Anthropic's published AI constitution.

Argues the document's function is to anchor identity and speed judgment rather than enforce rigid behavior, making coherent decisions cheaper because the reasoning doesn't have to be redone from scratch under stress.

Demonstrates the framework with a worked example, filtering seven stress-response options against competing principles until the one satisfying the most principles at once (cooking) emerges as the coherent choice.

Extends the concept to family life, describing a simple household principle ('we don't scream or get violent with one another') as an informal family constitution modeled for children during conflict.
quotes: I believe in what I call bottom-up agency, the ability to self-govern and take aligned action at any systemic level, which is compatible with top-down governance in systems.

A personal constitution is nothing different from an organizational one. I like to think of a personal constitution as a document containing these three elements: A mission, A set of principles, A personal declaration.

Amazon uses their Leadership Principles to rule the business from the bottom up: every member of the company uses this set of principles to make decisions or to settle tension when making a decision that affects the business.
What we are borrowing from legal constitutions is the idea of this set being an instrument that helps anchor identity and guide judgment rather than enforce behavior.

When you know what your direction is, it's easier to notice when you are off track. And when you know that you are off track, it's always good to have a reminder of what principles we can follow to return.
